headline: Gadi Eisenkot accepts Israel's mandate and calls for a national emergency government
standfirst: The former army chief has reached out to Likud, but his own bloc counts only 48 members. A Houthi attack damages an Aramco tower in Riyadh, Ukraine suffers fresh blackouts before the Abu Dhabi talks and COP31 opens in Antalya.

essentials.title: Gadi Eisenkot accepts the mandate in Israel and calls for a national emergency government
essentials.standfirst: The former army chief was formally asked on Sunday to form a government, with 67 recommendations but a bloc of only 48 members. He has invited Likud to join him and set four conditions for any partner.
body: On Sunday 8 November, at the presidential residence in Jerusalem, Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, formally handed Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, the mandate to form the next government, a day after announcing his choice.

Recommended by 67 of the Knesset's 120 members, against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu, the former chief of staff commands a bloc of only 48 and has promised creative, unconventional political moves to build a national emergency government.
He has until 6 December, extendable to 20 December, to assemble a majority, while the new members are due to be sworn in on Tuesday and Mr Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister.

vote.title: Parliamentary election
vote.system: Nationwide party-list proportional representation for the Knesset's 120 seats.

items.if: Gadi Eisenkot musters 61 members in time
items.then: he becomes prime minister, succeeding Benjamin Netanyahu, who is serving in a caretaker capacity.
Isaac Herzog can name another candidate; should that also fail, a majority of members can put forward a third, who has 14 days.
a fresh election is held within 90 days, with Benjamin Netanyahu remaining interim prime minister.

analysis.title: An open door for Likud
analysis.text: In his speech Mr Eisenkot did not mention Benjamin Netanyahu by name, but invited Likud and the Religious Zionist Party to join his coalition, saying his door was open. He set four conditions for any partner: recognising Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, respecting the values of its declaration of independence, accepting compulsory military or civilian service and committing to destroy Hamas, which he called a terrorist organisation. He made no mention of Otzma Yehudit, with which his deputy, Yoram Cohen, has ruled out governing. According to the Times of Israel, the most commonly cited arithmetic remains a 61-vote majority resting on his bloc, the seven members of United Torah Judaism and benign abstention by Shas.

keys.title: Isaac Herzog's message
keys.text: The head of state called for a stable government, able to withstand the threats from Iran, Gaza and Lebanon over the long term. He urged Mr Eisenkot to do everything he could to succeed.

keys.title: The Netanyahu camp
keys.text: The outgoing prime minister, who remains in office in a caretaker capacity, wants a national unity government with the right and the ultra-Orthodox parties. On Saturday he described the Arab parties as supporters of terrorism, a message Yashar called hysterical.

keys.title: The timetable
keys.text: Once his coalition is formed, Mr Eisenkot will have seven days to present it to the Knesset. His bloc first wants to replace the Speaker, Amir Ohana, which is not expected before next week, according to Israel Hayom.

context.t: Hamas attacks southern Israel, setting off the war in Gaza.
Parliamentary election: no bloc wins a majority.
Isaac Herzog says he will ask Gadi Eisenkot to form the government.
The mandate is formally handed over in Jerusalem; Mr Eisenkot reaches out to Likud.
The new Knesset is sworn in.
End of the initial 28-day deadline to form a government.

essentials.title: Houthi attack damages an Aramco tower in the heart of Riyadh's financial district
essentials.standfirst: Missiles fired from Yemen were intercepted over the Saudi capital on Sunday, but debris struck a building belonging to the oil giant. The Houthi authorities accuse Saudi aircraft of killing dozens of people near Sanaa.
body: Overnight on Saturday 7 and Sunday 8 November Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi missiles fired at Riyadh, but debris blew out the windows of several floors of an Aramco building in the King Abdullah Financial District, causing no casualties, according to the energy ministry.

The Iran-aligned Yemeni rebels have stepped up their fire on the kingdom's ports and airports since September, and their spokesman, Yahya Saree, claims they also targeted Riyadh's international airport, which the Saudi authorities have not confirmed.

The Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed missile launchers in Saada and Sanaa, while the Houthi-run health ministry reports at least 33 people killed on Saturday and 40 on Sunday in Saudi strikes near the Yemeni capital.

analysis.title: Another front in a regional war
analysis.text: According to Reuters, the Houthi offensive against the kingdom amounts to a new front in the war that America and Israel have waged on Iran since February. After advancing towards the Bab al-Mandab strait in September, the rebels have fired a growing number of missiles and drones at Saudi infrastructure; on 10 October an attack on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people, according to CBS News. The Houthis also claim strikes on Aramco storage tanks in Riyadh and Abqaiq, which the Institute for the Study of War has been unable to verify. Meanwhile Iran's Revolutionary Guards have targeted ships in the Strait of Hormuz, keeping up the pressure on the world's oil supply.

keys.title: The Eastern Province
keys.text: No disruption to Aramco's operations has been reported, according to Investing.com. Alerts were lifted on Sunday in Dhahran, Dammam, Abqaiq and Al-Ahsa, shortly before the interception of a missile aimed at the region was announced.

keys.title: Regional diplomacy
keys.text: According to Reuters, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials, whose countries are bound by a defence pact, met Iranian leaders in Tehran last month. In October Britain announced defensive missions by its fighter jets.

essentials.title: In Ukraine 850,000 people lose power ahead of the talks in Abu Dhabi
essentials.standfirst: Fresh Russian strikes hit the power grid on Sunday, notably in the Dnipropetrovsk region, and the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant lost its external power supply. Paris says Europeans will take part in the talks on 10 and 11 November.
body: Overnight Russian strikes on Sunday 8 November left more than 850,000 people in Ukraine without electricity, over 600,000 of them in the Dnipropetrovsk region, according to the energy company DTEK, while one person was killed and three wounded in Dnipro.

The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant lost its external power and is running on diesel generators, and a drone hit the site in Komyshuvakha where an earlier strike killed at least 55 people, targeting rescuers, according to Kyiv.

France's foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, announced that France and other Europeans would join the talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, which had until now been conceived as a meeting between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.

analysis.title: Winter as a weapon
analysis.text: Moscow is pressing on with its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid as winter approaches. Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia fired 115 missiles, nearly 1,900 guided bombs and more than 3,000 attack drones in a single week. Russia's defence ministry says it hit a substation supplying firms in the military-industrial complex. In the Zhytomyr region 140 apartment blocks were left without heating, and in the Kharkiv region up to 250,000 customers lost power, since restored. The loss of external power at the Zaporizhzhia plant, after the Ferosplavna line was disconnected, revives fears over the safety of Europe's largest nuclear site, which now depends on its back-up generators.

keys.title: Komyshuvakha
keys.text: The Russian drone hit the former school and a nearby shelter that had already been struck on Monday, injuring no one, according to the emergency services. Volodymyr Zelensky denounced what he called absolute cynicism.

keys.title: The Abu Dhabi format
keys.text: The talks had been presented as a three-way meeting organised by Washington. Jean-Noël Barrot did not say who would represent France.

essentials.title: COP31 opens in Antalya as the world looks set to overshoot 1.5°C
essentials.standfirst: Nearly 200 countries meet in Turkey until 20 November for the UN climate conference, presided over by Ankara with Australia leading the negotiations. Current policies point to 2.8°C of warming, according to the UN's latest projection.
body: The 31st UN climate conference opens on Monday 9 November in Antalya, Turkey, bringing together delegations from nearly 200 countries until 20 November under the presidency of Turkey's environment minister, Murat Kurum.

Scientists consider it almost certain that warming will exceed 1.5°C in 2026, and current policies point to a rise of 2.8°C by the end of the century, according to the UN's latest projection, cited by the German news agency DPA.

Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, will chair the negotiations, an unprecedented division of roles, ahead of a leaders' summit on 11 and 12 November at which markedly fewer heads of state are expected than at recent COPs.

analysis.title: A two-headed presidency
analysis.text: Turkey and Australia both bid to host the conference; the compromise reached in November 2025 gave Ankara the organisation and the action agenda, and Canberra the conduct of the negotiations. DPA notes that this novel arrangement has raised fears of friction, as the two countries' proposals were poorly co-ordinated during the preparations. The chosen theme, implementation and acceleration, signals more modest ambitions: according to the UN's synthesis of plans from 154 countries, national pledges would cut emissions only about 6% below 2019 levels by 2035. Adaptation finance, which COP30 in Belém promised to triple, looks set to be one of the main sticking points.

keys.title: Fewer leaders
keys.text: A provisional UN list has 77 heads of state or government registered to speak, against 116 in Dubai in 2023, according to Climate & Capital Media. Turkey says it expects 91 leaders.

keys.title: The hosts and coal
keys.text: Greenpeace criticises Turkey for its coal subsidies and a plan to expand a power station. Both host countries are still developing coal, according to the NGO Urgewald.

context.t: The Paris agreement is adopted, aiming to limit warming to 1.5°C.

essentials.title: Myanmar's army kills eleven people in an air strike on a school in Sagaing
essentials.standfirst: Teachers and children were among the victims of a bombing on Saturday in Kani township, according to independent Burmese media. The National Unity Government counted 641 army air strikes in October.
body: At around 11.30am on Saturday 7 November an air strike by Myanmar's army hit a school and the village of Nyaung Pin Le, in Kani township in the Sagaing region, killing eleven people, most of them teachers and children, according to independent media.

The bombing is part of an air campaign that killed 212 civilians in October, 23 of them children, according to the exiled National Unity Government, nearly six years after the coup and seven months after Min Aung Hlaing was elected president.

Fighting continues in Mon State, where more than 15,000 residents have fled Kyaikto township, and in Rakhine, while from 9 November the army is closing checkpoints at night in three Sagaing townships.

analysis.title: War from the air
analysis.text: Unable to retake large swathes of the countryside, the army relies on its air force, which the resistance has no means to counter. Sagaing, the heartland of armed opposition to the 2021 coup, is the worst-hit region: besides the school in Kani, a hospital in Kawlin township was bombed on 4 November, killing at least 12 people including a doctor, and a shelter for displaced people was hit in Wetlet. Min Aung Hlaing's election as president in April, after a vote organised by the army, has not ended the fighting. Shells fired in Karen State have also landed in Thailand's Tak province, damaging homes.

keys.title: The American channel
keys.text: America opened direct negotiations with the military government in October, while keeping its sanctions on Min Aung Hlaing. On 3 November the National Unity Government responded to an American strategy document.

keys.title: Prosecutions
keys.text: A Philippine appeals court has registered a petition from the Chin Human Rights Organization targeting Min Aung Hlaing and nine other officers, according to the NGO.

brief.text: An earthquake of magnitude 5.7, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, centred in Shizuoka prefecture, injured at least 22 people in central Japan, according to local media cited by the AP.
Pope Leo XIV preached to some 40,000 worshippers in Paysandú, on the Argentine border, during a 12-day tour of South America that ends on 17 November.

Donald Trump called a new offensive against Iran very unlikely, while linking it to progress in talks, and said the Iron Gate task force, meant to cut Iran's overland arms routes, was fully operational.
The UAE's National Guard rescued 22 people after a cargo ship caught fire in the Gulf of Oman, as attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz multiply.
